newsitem.title: USA: Two unions approve Ketchikan Pulp closure pact.
newsitem.headline: Two unions approve Ketchikan Pulp closure pact.

text.p: Two of the three unions representing workers at the Ketchikan Pulp Co mill in Ketchikan, Alaska, have signed closure agreements approving the company's severance package, the Louisiana-Pacific Corp subsidiary said on Thursday.

Louisiana-Pacific said Monday it would close the mill at the end of March. The plant, built in the 1950s, has been losing money and was forecast to lose more than $40 million this year, company officials said.
Ketchikan Pulp unveiled a severance package on Wednesday that offers two weeks' pay for each year of continuous service, or four weeks' pay for each employee's last permanent job classification.
The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers (IBEW) and the International Union of Operating Engineers (IUOE) agreed to the package on Thursday, Ketchikan Pulp said.
Both unions had lobbied on behalf of Ketchikan Pulp to extend the company's controversial supply contract for Tongass National Forest timber.
The Clinton administration and Congress rejected the proposal, which would have tacked 15 years on to the 50-year contract, now due to expire in 2004.

Louisiana-Pacific said that without the extension it could not justify investing the approximately $180 million needed to bring the plant up to current environmental standards and to improve efficiency.
Much of that investment was mandated by consent decrees issued in 1995 criminal and civil settlements over federal pollution charges.

Critics have blasted the contract as a government subsidy for an uncompetitive operation that degrades the temperate rain forest of the Tongass. But company officials blamed environmentalists for the impending mill closure.

"We're looking forward to efficient, environmentally sound operations through the winter. It is terribly sad that people can't recognize the great strides KPC has made in our operations and the value of family-wage employment we have provided," said Ketchikan Pulp Personnel and Labor Relations Manager Amy Sullivan in a news release.
Union representatives also lamented the mill's impending closure.
Ketchikan Pulp said it hoped to get approval of the severance package from the third union by November 4.
The mill produces dissolving pulp, a material used to make rayon, cellophane and other industrial materials.
The company, with about 500 pulp mill workers and about 500 saw mill workers, is the largest private employer for Ketchikan, a city of 14,000 on the tip of the southeast Alaska panhandle.

Ketchikan Pulp's workforce is 80 percent male, with an average annual pay of $46,100 and average longevity of more than nine years, according to a recent study commissioned by the Ketchikan Gateway Borough.
According to the August study, 42 percent of the workers planned to move away from Ketchikan permanently if the mill closed.
The company has said it plans to keep its two southeast Alaska saw mills operating after the pulp mill closes.
This week it began negotiations with the U.S. Forest Service for a guaranteed Tongass timber supply to feed the saw mills, which have a combined annual capacity of 110 million board feet.
